Nikola Tesla Finds Capacity of Electrical Conductor Not Constant.
Makes a Study of a Phenomenon Which Results in Revealing an Error in the Accepted Theories of Electrical Laws.
Nikola Tesla has announced another new discovery in electricity. This time it is a new law, and by reason of it Mr. Tesla asserts a large part of technical literature will have to be rewritten. Ever since anything has been known about electricity, scientific men have taken for granted that the capacity of an electrical conductor is constant. When Tesla was experimenting in Colorado he found this capacity is not constant, but variable. Then he determined to find out the law governing this phenomenon. He said:
“It is well known that an electric circuit comports itself like a spring with a weight attached to it. Such a spring vibrates at a definite rate, which is determined by two quantities, the pliability of the spring and the mass of the weight. Similarly an electric circuit vibrates, and its vibration, too, is dependent on two qualities, designated as electrostatic capacity and inductance. The capacity of the electric circuit corresponds to the pliability of the spring and the inductance to the mass of weight.

Discredits Tesla's Martian Theory
New York Herald
January 5th, 1901
Mr. Marconi Attributes Alleged Messages from Mars to Local Atmospheric Disturbances.
[SPECIAL CABLE TO THE HERALD.]
The Herald 's European edition publishes the following from its correspondent:—
LONDON, Saturday.— Nikola Tesla having set up the fascinating, or fantastic, theory as to the possibility of communicating with the people of Mars, the Daily Mail yesterday sought the opinion of Mr. Marconi, who is conducting experiments in wireless telegraphy near Poole, and Mr. Marconi gave the following reply:—
"In earlier experiments, before my apparatus was perfected, I often received signals apparently from nowhere. This was undoubtedly due to atmospheric electricity. One of the greatest difficulties has been to produce an apparatus which would eliminate them, but this I have lately succeeded in doing.
"I should attribute the alleged signals from Mars to local disturbances in the atmosphere."
Professor Fleming, F. R. S., of University College, laughed at the idea of communicating with Mars, even if there are any people there.
"Is this idea taken seriously?" was his first question. "I am afraid," added the distinguished authority on electrical science, "that Tesla has been led away by his own imagination. It is difficult, of course, to say that anything is beyond the ultimate reach of science, but at present I should say that the people of Mars are."

Hanging a Thing of the Past
From The Brooklyn Eagle .
One thing at least is reasonably sure: We shall not go back to the old bungling, barbarous, brutal and uncertain hanging. Execution by electricity is appropriate to the age we live in. It does not make a revolting scene like a hanging. It is accompanied by no noise and disturbance. It is instant in its action and a stout neck or a strong physique does not prolong the death into an agony that must seem to the victim to endure for ages. Nor is the victim usually inspired by the terror and physical fear that overcome him at the sight of weapons or axes or a gallows. We are not for coddling criminals, by any means, but when we put them out of the world we can afford to do it in a rapid and businesslike way. The sentence of the law for murder is death, not torture.

Gov. Flower says in an interview that he will aid in an effort to determine whether electricity actually kills condemned persons, if he can legally do so. There is a reasonable doubt as to the efficacy of the electrical current as an agent of death; and that doubt should be removed as soon as possible, if electrical shock is to continue the legal method of execution in this State.
The law which provides for electrocution was framed by the friends of the method, and contained provisions that rendered death certain after all the formalities had been observed, whether the victim succumbed to the shock or not. After the electrical current has done the work expected, the body must be legally cut up by physicians, thus ending all chance of a return to consciousness. Marconi and Prof. Fleming Doubt That Any Signals Come From Mars.
Special Cable Despatch to THE SUN.
London, Jan. 5. — The Sun’s interview with Nikola Tesla in regard to his experiments in Colorado and the possibility of communicating with inhabitants of the planets has aroused widespread interest in England.
Two expert criticisms have appeared so far. Signor Marconi declares that he often received mysterious signals until he had perfected his apparatus. He attributes these signals to atmospheric electricity. He considers Nikola Tesla’s signals due to local atmospheric disturbances, which are especially prevalent at a high altitude. This criticism is obviously open to criticism itself, ignoring as it does the intelligent and constant nature of the signals recorded by Nikola Tesla’s instrument, which removes them from the category of irregular, “apparently from nowhere,” signals. Moreover, in regard to Marconi, a touch of professional rivalry cannot but be suspected in the implication that Marconi’s apparatus is perfect while Nikola Tesla’s is not.

by R. James McCabe
ExtraOrdinary Technology
October, 2006
Page number(s):
42
Many researchers have noticed that Tesla's Patent No. 1,119,732 1 has a huge donut type antenna at the top of the tower. When Nikola built his Wardenclyffe wireless tower on Long
Island, New York, the donut was replaced by a dome or mushroom design.
There has been speculation as to why the change…
Is the dome just a better design?
Perhaps there is a benefit to having a large interior cavity at the top of the tower?
As usual the real reason isn't all that exciting. The original donut design was very expensive. The architects' presented Tesla with an estimate of $450,000 1 for the donut antenna. Tesla had to change the antenna to a more economical design.
—RJM

Doubts Value of Tesla Discovery
New York Herald
November 9th, 1898
Professor C. F. Brackett Says Electrical Scientist's Invention Would Not Work in Practice
Denies Its Originality
Asserts That Naval Warfare Cannot Be Terminated in the Manner Suggested by the Inventor
A. S. Brown Less Doubtful
Declares He Has Full Faith in the Inventor's Ability to Carry Out His Ideas
Nikola Tesla's declaration, made in yesterday's HERALD, that he had discovered a system of applying an electrical current whereby such marvellous results might be obtained as the destruction of battle ships, balloons or land vehicles at a great distance, attracted deep interest not only on the part of the general public, but among electrical experts and scientists. In some quarters doubt was expressed as to the possibility of Tesla putting his invention to practical use. Others were confident that the inventor would in time be able to make good his declaration by practical demonstration.
One of those inclined to question the value of Tesla's discovery was Cyrus F. Brackett, professor of physics in Princeton University and head of the Henry electrical school of Princeton, N. J., who is author of a treatise on physics.

Dr. Nikola Tesla and His Achievements
by Samuel Cohen
Electrical Experimenter
February, 1917
Page number(s):
712, 713, 777
Perhaps the ever-broadening field of invention has never known a genius more successful in developing far-reaching and original inventions than Dr. Nikola Tesla, whose name is known in every corner of the globe for his scientific achievements.
Dr. Tesla was born in 1857 in Smiljan, Lika, border country of Austria-Hungary, His early education was obtained in the elementary school of his native place. He continued his studies in the public school in Gospic, Lika, and after spending a period of four years in the Lower Real School in Croatia, he graduated in 1873.
His parents originally desired him to study for the clergy, which can be readily understood when one considers that Dr. Tesla's father was himself a very noted clergyman and orator. However, young Tesla had his mind set on mathematics and physics, and after prevailing upon his parents for permission to study engineering, he entered the Polytechnic School at Gratz, where for four years he studied mathematics, physics and mechanics, after which followed a two year course in philosophic studies at the University of Prague, Bohemia. Ten years ago, on the 7th of January, 1943, Dr. Nikola Tesla, died in New York City. He was perhaps one of the most controversial figures in the fields of science. Dr. Tesla, at 77, Seldom Sleeps
New York Times
July 11th, 1933
Page number(s):
19
Inventor Says His Health and Mind Are Better Than Ever — Expects to Live Beyond 140.
WORKING ON A NEW STEEL
To Be Twice as Strong as at Present — Assails 'Pad and Pencil Scientists.'
Nikola Tesla, dean of American inventors, with a hundred triumphs in electrical engineering behind him, was 77 years old yesterday. In an interview at the Hotel Governor Clinton, where he lives, he said he was in better health and more alert mentally than ever before in his life...
He sketched the regimen by which he expects to live scores of years more. It includes virtually no sleep and rigidly limited meals. He also told of further work on inventions that he believes may revolutionize the world.
On his birthday last year Dr. Tesla announced he was working on a new source of energy, but yesterday he said he had concentrated, for financial reasons, on work in molecular physics. He was confident it would make possible the economical production of enormously improved metals. His researches would apply to all metals, but principally steel, he said.
"I am hoping to produce a steel, at the same cost as present steel, so much better that a building such as the Empire State could be built with one-half the amount of steel now required. Dr. Tesla, 82 Today, Postpones Party
New York Times
July 10th, 1938
Wants to Finish Therapeutic Device Which He Calls Boon for Newspaper Offices
For the first time in a number of years, Dr. Nikola Tesla, scientist and inventor, who is 82 years old today, is postponing his annual birthday party for the press so he may complete a mechanical therapeutic device for public demonstration.
Dr. Tesla said yesterday he hopes to have his apparatus completed within two weeks, and then will give a demonstration to the press.
For the last forty years Dr. Tesla has been the storm center of scientific controversy. Recognized in the early part of his career as the father of modern methods of generating and distributing electrical energy, and pre-dating even Marconi in his experiments with wireless, Dr. Tesla has been decorated by many governments for his accomplishments. In recent years, however, it has been his custom to announce at his annual parties the perfection of inventions which some scientists have challenged as fantastic.
The therapeutic device, Dr. Tesla said yesterday, is an improvement of an invention he perfected many years ago before his famous laboratory burned, about 1895. He said it will cure many internal disorders. He used it to advantage on his friend, Mark Twain, Dr. Tesla said.
"One of these devices in every newspaper office and the proverbial ‘editorial grouch' will be gone," the inventor predicted.

Dr. Tesla Claims New Discoveries
Modern Mechanix
October, 1935
Dr. Nikola Tesla is shown here as he was being interviewed by the press on his discovery of an apparatus for transmitting energy to any distance. He kept the details secret.
Claiming that the propositions of relativity are false, and asserting that he has discovered a new apparatus for transmitting mechanical energy without wires and to any distance, Dr. Nikola Tesla, world famous scientist made formal announcement of his discoveries on his 79th birthday recently.
Should his announced energy transmitter prove successful, it would become the most sought for device in the world.

Dr. Tesla Finds Ray to Kill Army at 100-Mile Distance
Binghamton Press
July 11th, 1934
Page number(s):
1
Discovery Reported to Make Defense Impregnable; Plans Gift to Arms Parley
New York, July 11 — (Associated Press) — The discovery of a force ray that would destroy an army 100 miles away, that would make A nation's defenses Impregnable, has been announced by the inventor, Dr. Nikola Tesla.
In the interests of peace, Dr. Tesla said he plans to place the ray at the disposal of the Geneva disarmament conference. He announced the invention yesterday, on the occasion of his 75th birthday.
The force ray, Dr. Tesla said, would consist of particles, driven electrically and projected in vast curtains, miles high and 100 miles long.
The speed of the particles — traveling at velocities of 50,000,000 volts — was described by him as giving the ray its destructive powers.
He said projecting plants, set up every 200 miles along a border, each shooting rays 100 miles on each side, would make the border impenetrable.
A fleet of 10,000 airplanes, flying into such a curtain, he said, would be destroyed.

Dr. Tesla Gives Home to an Errant Pigeon That Flew Into 40th-Story Room in Hotel
New York Times
February 6th, 1935
Early yesterday morning, not so long after it started snowing, an apologetic housekeeper on the fortieth floor of the Hotel New Yorker — one flight from the roof — telephoned down to the office that there was a bird in one of the unoccupied rooms. Apparently it had flown in a window which had been left partially open during the night, she explained.
When the management arrived on the scene the "bird" was perched on the top of a dresser, as unaccountable as Poe's raven, and twice as ambiguous. It was a homing pigeon with a leg band reading: "I. F. 34 N. U. 1286," and it seemed to have just got in after a long hard flight. It was caught and shut in a bathroom until its legband could be deciphered.
The news of it spread, however. At 7 o'clock, while the management was still trying to face the anomaly of the homing pigeons without a home, a chambermaid was repeating the story to Dr. Nikola Tesla, the 78-year-old scientist, in his thirty-third floor suite. Dr. Tesla, who is fond of pigeons, as the chambermaid knows from experience, promptly called the management and volunteered to take charge of the foundling.

Dr. Tesla Talks of Gas Turbines
by Nikola Tesla
Motor World
September 18th, 1911
Page number(s):
23, 37
So Confident, He Offers to Build Them for Motor Cars
Considers New Power His Greatest Invention.
Gas turbines of practical and efficient construction, light, flexible and in every way suitable for automobile propulsion, are not a dream of the future only but a probability of only a very few years hence. At least such is the conviction of Dr. Nikola Tesla, whose newly developed method of fluid propulsion, as he calls it, and which was illustrated and described in last week's Motor World, is attracting so much attention in scientific circles. Dr. Tesla himself considers it the greatest of all his inventions. By his own statement the scientist already has built, run and carefully tested internal combustion engines operating on the new turbine principle and so confident is he of the thorough practicability of the idea that on Friday of last week he informed a Motor World man that he would even be willing today to sign a contract to build and install turbines for automobiles. He readily admits, however, that he would like to have more time, considerable more time probably, in which to develop a method of combustion entirely suited to the turbine.

by Helen Welshimer
Every Week Magazine
October 21st, 1934

The famous inventor's new beam of death could bring down a fleet of 10,000 planes at a distance of 250 miles, he claims, and it also would make obsolete the submarine.
"America Enters War!"
"United Stated Joins Allies!"
"Congress Declares War!"
The newsboys were screaming the headlines through the rainy April night. Men and women stood on corners, talking, talking, talking—
The drift of the days went on. Troop trains pulled out of the stations, from Centreville, Mississippi, up to Bangor, Maine. The drums throbbed and the trumpets blew. The ships sailed and the casualty lists came back. One by one, the gold stars replaced the white—
And 1917 drifted into 1918.
Dr. Nikola Tesla was in his laboratory trying hard to solve a problem of ages. Once in a while he raised his head to listen. Then he turned back to his experiments. He was going to end war!
The noted inventor, 78 years old now, already had 700 inventions to his credit. This was to be his greatest.
Years marched on. The fanfare and the drums were done. The dead were buried. The living came home.

To the New York Herald Tribune:
I have been a reader of your excellent paper for more than fifty years and feel much obliged to you for the pleasure and enlightenment derived from its perusal. Many of your admirable editorials are on my files. Under these circumstances it is unfortunate that your issue of Sunday, July 11, contained a report very injurious to me.
The particularly damaging statement is: "The decorations made very little impression on Dr. Tesla. 'They mean nothing - take them away,' said Dr. Tesla."
I should say that the expression on my face in the photograph accompanying the report, would be sufficient to disprove the above assertion. When it became necessary to clear the table I was very anxious that the precious objects be placed in safe hands and requested my old friend, George Scherff, auditor of the Union Sulphur Company, who was one of the honored guests, to take care of them. The Drama of Mr. Tesla
New York Herald Tribune
January 17th, 1943
Page number(s):
A8
Mr. Nikola Tesla, the "wizard," died the other day, and he left a lot of questions unanswered. His solid accomplishments were astonishing in their scope-more than nine hundred patents, including the transforming coil and the induction motor. But, important as were his accomplishments, he deserves attention as a dreamer. He had! always been absorbed by glimpses into the world of tomorrow, a world in which power would be transmitted by radio, in which science could make the desert blossom by what would amount to the touching of a button. Early Decision is Necessary for Preserving Adams Plant
Niagara Falls Gazette
December 29th, 1961
Time is growing short for a decision on the future — if there is to be any future — of the Edward Dean Adams power station on the upper Niagara River.
This ancient hydroelectric plant is the daddy of them all. It was the Adams plant which first transmitted alternating current 25 miles to Buffalo in 1896. This was accomplished because of the efforts of Nikola Tesla, who developed the polyphase alternating current motor, and George Westinghouse, who adapted the system for the Adams generators.
Some time next fall the Adams plant will be taken out of service for all time. It will no longer be needed.
It would be unfortunate if it were to be torn down or left idle and forgotten. It is a symbol of the electrical age. It deserves to be preserved and maintained as a museum or electrical hall of fame, call it what you will. The buildings could be adapted to provide space for a permanent industrial exhibit.
Niagara Falls would derive benefit from having such a showplace to add to attractions for visitors. Museums are doing very well in Cooperstown and other tourist centers.
Surely, there are people in the community and in the American electrical industry with the imagination and leadership to undertake such a project.

Edison and His Inventions
Yonkers Statesman
July 22nd, 1892
The story that Mr. Edison has invented something by which a city could be destroyed, for instance, by an enemy thirty miles away, is, of course, an absurdity. The only interesting thing about it is that it is generally believed in Europe that Edison has perfected some such wholesale agent of destruction. He has received in the past two or three months a number of letters, some of them from people in authority, asking what there is in the report, and one of the letters contained an intimation that an European government might be disposed to treat with him for the exclusive possession of the secret.
Mr. Edison has told his friends about this experience, and has added that he has but one secret, and that is the operation of his ore extractor, a secret which he expects will yield him several millions of dollars.
Whether the fairy-like suggestion of his that an enemy might be destroyed by an electrically-charged volume of water played from a hose, or whether the report was due to the the suggestion that the discovery of Nikola Tesla might be utilized in war, so as to cast a lightning bolt into an enemy’s town or upon an enemy’s ship, Mr. Edison does not know, but he is inclined to think that the report can be traced to one of these two sources.

These prizes have been regularly awarded since 1901, and the learned Academies of Sweden while admittedly well informed and fair as to the award of the prize, have in the past, we believe, overlooked several scientists who by all means were entitled to the prize long ere this.

Electric Journal
June, 1919
In February, 1904, a fund was provided and a deed of gift creating the Edison Medal executed between twenty-three individuals and the New York Trust Company, such deed being amended in March, 1908, to include as one of the parties thereto the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, whereby it was provided, ameng other things, as follows:—
"The Institute shall, through a Committee to be duly appointed and authorized by it and known as The Edison Medal Committee, cause a gold medal to be executed from said die, or according to said design and specifications, and shall award said medal to some one resident of the United States of America and its Dependencies, or of the
Dominion of Canada for "Meritorious Achievement" in Electrical Science or Electrical Engineering or the Electrical Arts, whenever in the judgment of said Committee a resident of either of said countries is properly deserving of such award; provided, nevertheless, the requisite funds have accrued from said investment to so be made by the Trust Company."
In compliance with the obligation assumed by it the American Institute of Electrical Engineers in May, 1909, approved a set of by-laws of The Edison Medal Committee creating the machinery and prescribing the method of procedure to be thereafter followed in awarding the Edison Medal. Edison Outdone
Boulder Daily Camera
March 4th, 1896
Page number(s):
2
Wizard Tesla Substitutes Dilute Air for Electric Light Filaments.
A more original genius than Edison, veritably a wizard, is his young disciple, Nikola Tesla, who was born in Servia, and found employment with Edison on landing in America. For small electric lights he dispenses with the filaments inside the bulbs, and makes dilute air do their work. He sends currents of high tension through space, without any conductor, at a voltage many times greater than that employed in electrocution. He receives in his person currents vibrating a million times a second, of two hundred times greater voltage than needed to produce death. He surrounds himself with a halo of electric light, and calls purple streams from the soil. His experiments are of the utmost promise to the industrial world. His aim is to hook man's machinery directly to nature's, pressing the ether waves directly into our service without the intervention or the generation of heat, in which such an enormous proportion of the energy goes to waste - 90 per cent in arc lighting, 94 in incandescent. - Pres. Andrews in Scribner's.

They backed going wireless, underground
BY JILL JONNES
NEW YORK TIMES NEWS SERVICE
BALTIMORE — The immortals of electricity, in their shimmering Valhalla, must have had a pretty amusing couple of months.
First they got to cackle over the Northeast blackout, wherein tens of millions of denizens of the 21st century were rudely reminded of their slavish dependence upon this late-19th-century technology.
A few weeks later, in roared Hurricane Isabel, wiping out electric service in huge swaths in the mid-Atlantic. Millions lost power, some for more than a week. Trains came to a standstill; lights, computers and televisions went dark; air conditioning and refrigerators ceased cooling, and coffee makers gurgled into distressing silence.
Without electricity, a caffeinated, computer-driven civilization careened to a halt.
And then, just for good measure, practically all of Italy was zapped perhaps, reports suggested, by something as prosaic as trees falling on transmission wires.
Thomas Edison, inventor of the incandescent light bulb and the first electrical grid, would have his own reasons for gloating. If the world had only listened to him in the 1890s, there would not be endless miles of transmission lines vulnerable to falling trees. Rome Citizen
June 9th, 1896

Whatever may be the facts in regard to Nikola Tesla's reported invention of a new system of electric lighting, there seems to be no doubt that Edison has got hold of a really practical improvement in electric lighting that is as great an advance over the present incandescent lamp as that was over coal gas. The new light is produced by the introduction of electricity into a partial vacuum within a globe composed of glass in which the crystals of a certain mineral have been fused so as to form an interior coating looking like frosting. The diagram herewith shown gives the form of the new lamp. It will be seen that there is no carbon loop. The electric current, entering at the points A and B, sets in motion the molecules of air within the globe, which are driven against the mineral-coated surface and deflected, as shown by the dotted lines, the molecules agitated at A taking the course D, E, F, G, and those agitated by the current entering at B taking the opposite direction. This produces a perfectly white light, much more powerful than the present incandescent lamp. The only difficulty in the way of the success of the new light is in the cracking of the crystals. Edison expects to overcome this very soon, when the public will be afforded a much cheaper and more powerful electric light than at present in bulbs which will be practically indestructible. Electrical World
March 21st, 1896

BY EDWIN J. HOUSTON AND A. E. KENNELLY.
Mr. Thomas A. Edison, after numerous experiments on the Röntgen rays with about 150 different glass vacuum tubes, has communicated the following information to us for publication:
First. There is no apparent advantage in obtaining a very high vacuum in the Crookes tubes employed for obtaining shadowgraphs of metal gratings. The effect of a very high vacuum is to require a greater voltage to produce fluorescence. The best degree of vacuum seems to be that at which the internal luminescence or stria in the tube just disappear and fluorescence of the walls remains. The Röntgen rays are still produced even when internal striæ are observed, but are then much enfeebled.
Second. Thin walls are preferable to thick walls in the glass vacuum tubes. A thick wall will fluoresce more noticeably and become very hot. A thin wall will emit rays upon the photographic plate, but may scarcely fluoresce visibly and will remain very cool. This is proved by a number of experiments, of which the following is one: The tube of a shape roughly indicated in Fig. I has its walls blown thick in the zone of A C, but thin at B. When this tube is exhausted and excited, the thin part, B, which is in the most active area, remains cool and the radiographic power is active, while the glass becomes hot in the ring A C. The types of alternating-current apparatus which and the Polyare in use to-day have resulted from a process phase System of evolution which has been going on for many years and in which the polyphase induction motor has been the fundamental element. The announcement of the polyphase induction motor and of the polyphase system were made by Mr. Tesla in 1888. The motor excited much interest and expectation. The polyphase system received little consideration. The motor, however, was helpless without a supply of suitable current. The alternators of that day were single-phase, they gave 120 to 133 cycles; alternators and transformers were ill adapted for supplying out-of-phase current. Editorial Comments Regarding the Nikola Tesla Lecture in Chicago
Electrical World
September 2nd, 1893
Page number(s):
167
The lecture delivered by Mr. Tesla at Chicago on Friday evening of last week was a disappointment to those who expected to be entertained with brilliant experiments in luminous discharges, transmissions without wires, and other like subjects with which the name of Tesla is so intimately associated. In place of these experiments, his audience soon found out, what perhaps many of them did not know before, that the subject of the lecture was mechanical and electrical oscillators, a purely technical subject, involving but a few experiments, and these of little interest except to technical men; those of his audience who were not technical men were therefore disappointed; instead of being entertained they were being instructed with some matters not easily grasped by them. The apparatus forming the subject of his lecture was a true Tesla surprise, as will be seen from our brief report of the lecture. It consisted of a pneumatic oscillator, the underlying principle of which is analogous to that of the Leyden jar, the result accomplished being that it produced short, rapid, mechanical oscillations; but it differed in that these oscillations were of an absolutely constant frequency, as constant as that of a tuning fork, a feature which may make the apparatus quite a valuable one.

Editorial - The New Inventions of Tesla
Electrical Review and Western Electrician
May 20th, 1911
Page number(s):
978
The address made by Dr. Nikola Tesla before the New York Section of the National Electric Light Association this week, and reported upon other pages of this issue, is one which will attract great attention on account of the startling statements which were made by the speaker. Mr. Tesla has been working upon the inventions now announced for a number of years, and while it is impossible to estimate their importance until further details are made known, the claims made for transmitting energy and speech to great distances point to an epoch-making discovery.
The experiments made by Dr. Tesla upon high-frequency and high-potential currents about twenty years ago were most illuminating and opened a field of vast possibilities to both the scientist and the engineer - a field which is still being explored. His other discoveries have attracted considerable attention, and this latest announcement bids fair to prove the most important of all.
Aside from his work on electrical oscillations, Dr. Tesla has invented and constructed a prime mover for which remarkable results are claimed. A bronze bust of Nikola Tesla, U.S. electrical engineer and pioneer in the field of electric motors and radio communications, now graces the entryway to Davies Auditorium in the Becton Engineering and Applied Science Center, 15 Prospect St.. This is the second time the Croatian-born inventor has been honored by Yale. In 1894, he received an honorary degree from Yale along with several other 19th-century leaders.
The Tesla sculpture was funded through a letter-writing campaign by a classroom of third-graders in Ann Arbor, Michigan, under the leadership of their teacher, John Wagner , who presented the sculpture to Yale on April 21. The students practiced their penmanship by writing letters to more than 100 American corporation leaders seeking donations.
D. Allan Bromley, dean of Yale engineering, noted that Tesla's discovery of the rotating magnetic field in 1888 enabled him to invent and patent the first practical system for generating and transmitting alternating current. The discovery made it possible to transmit electricity long distances, surpassing the range of direct current transmissions. Tesla's many inventions included high- frequency generators for electric motors, 1890, and the Tesla coil, 1891, a transformer important for radio communications.

by Nikola Tesla
Electrical Engineer
August 26th, 1891
Page number(s):
233
In The Electrical Engineer of August 12 , I find some remarks of Prof. J. J. Thomson, which appeared originally in the London Electrician and which have a bearing upon some experiments described by me in your issue of July 1 .
I did not, as Prof. J. J. Thomson seems to believe, misunderstand his position in regard to the cause of the phenomena considered, but I thought that in his experiments, as well as in my own, electrostatic effects were of great importance. It did not appear, from the meagre description of his experiments, that all possible precautions had been taken to exclude these effects. I did not doubt that luminosity could be excited in a closed tube when electrostatic action is completely excluded. In fact, at the outset, I myself looked for a purely electrodynamic effect and believed that I had obtained it. But many experiments performed at that time proved to me that the electrostatic effects were generally of far greater importance, and admitted of a more satisfactory explanation of most of the phenomena observed.

August 12th, 1891

As was to be expected, the lecture delivered by Mr. Tesla in which he describes the illuminating effects observed in vacuum tubes, has called forth a number of communications from other experimenters who had, it appears, been working in the same direction. Mr. Tesla, it will be remembered, has succeeded in obtaining the effects observed by the employment of very high potential combined with a very high period of alternations, and ascribes the results as due almost, if not entirely, to electro-static action. Prof. J. J. Thomson, in his study of those phenomena, is led to the conclusion that luminosity in tubes without electrodes can be produced by electro-dynamic as well as by electro-static action. In proof of this he cites an experiment in which the electro-static action was ostensibly screened by covering the tube with wet blotting paper. It would seem doubtful, however, whether the precautions taken were sufficiently complete to avoid any electro-static action whatever, and for lack of further proof on this point final judgment may well be suspended. by Nikola Tesla
New York Herald
February 25th, 1917
The ideal simplicity of the induction motor, its perfect reversibility and other unique qualities render it eminently suitable for ship propulsion, and ever since I brought my system of power transmission to the attention of the profession through the American Institute of Electrical Engineers I have vigorously insisted on its application for that purpose. During many years the scheme was declared to be impracticable and I was assailed in a manner as vicious as incompetent. In 1900, when an article from me advocating the electric drive appeared in the Century Magazine, Marine Engineering pronounced the plan to be the "climax of asininity," and such was the fury aroused by my proposals that the editor of another technical periodical resigned and severed his connection rather than to allow the publication of some attacks.
A similar reception was accorded to my wireless boat repeatedly described in the Herald of 1898. The patents on these inventions have since expired and they are now common property. Meanwhile insane antagonism and ignorance have been replaced by helpful interest and appreciation of their value. Marvels That Nikola Tesla’s Visitors Saw the Other Night.
New York, Oct. 5. — Millions of volts of electricity were harnessed the other night in Nikola Tesla’s laboratory and turned into the plaything of men and women. The occasion was a reception given the members of the American Electro-Therapeutic Association by Mr. Tesla.
First was exhibited the machine for generating electricity, invented by Mr. Tesla. This machine looks something like an ordinary turning lathe, and with it a perfect control can be had over the vibration of the electrical current. The velocity of the movement is such that a shadow extending almost two inches from either end of the bar causes an appearance like the bar itself.
After this had been explained everybody was instructed to join a circle around a table which looked like an ordinary dining room article, but was heavily bound with wires. Spectator
February 6th, 1892
Page number(s):
193
If the beautiful experiments exhibited at the Royal Institution by Mr. Tesla, the able lieutenant of Mr. Edison, are of practical value, and not the mere playthings of the lecture-room, we may be on the eve of some of the greatest discoveries that the world has ever seen. What mankind want during the waking hours of the night is not a glow in the darkness, however intense, but a suffusing, pervading illumination. They want, in fact, sunshine at night. But this, it seems, is what Mr. Tesla is on the eve of offering to us. At his lectures at the Royal Institution, the following striking experiment was shown. It consisted "in joining two sheets of tinfoil, one over the lecturer's head, the other on the table, to the poles of his generator. The space between these two sheets immediately became electrified, and a long vacuum-tube waved about in it, without attachment to any conductor whatever, glowed in the darkness like a flaming sword. This experiment was intended to illustrate the possibility of rendering an entire room so electric, by plates in the ceiling or under the floor, that vacuum-bulbs placed anywhere within it would yield a light." In other words, we shall be able to fill our rooms with the potentiality of light, and then be able, by the simple introduction of vacuum-tubes, to obtain any quantity of light. Rival of the Edison Company Makes Reductions for Small and Large Consumers.
IS NOW AS CHEAP AS GAS
Wholesale Users Can Get Electricity at Even a Lower Price Than the Older Illuminant.
FURTHER CUTS POSSIBLE.
To meet the reduction in electric light rates made by the Edison Company on October 1, the United Electric Light and Power Company yesterday issued a new schedule, with a rate considerably lower than that of the rival company. This reduction, which will operate on bills for this month, places incandescent lights on the same footing with gas, practically, and large users will get the light even cheaper than gas.
An attempt was made last winter in the Legislature at Albany to make electric light companies lower the price for incandescent lighting from the one cent an hour basis per sixteen candle power lamp to a three-quarters of a cent basis, but the bill did not become a law. Now the companies have made a cut voluntarily.
Likely to Affect Gas Companies.
This reduction, made by the two electric lighting companies, is the result, in a way, of a war between them, but the effect, it is said, will be felt the most by the gas companies. UTICA, March 22. — Papers have been filed in the United States court here in a case entitled "The Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company against the General Electric Company." and it is set down for trial April 4. The morning papers set forth that in 1889 the Westinghouse company acquired the exclusive control of the patents of Nikola Tesla known as the "Multiphase system." America is by far the largest user of electric light, but the methods of production and utilization in use here do not appear to be quite so economical as those practised abroad. The plants throughout Europe are generally on a much more modest scale than here, except in a few such cities as Berlin, Hamburg, and Vienna, yet recent statistics show that some of the smallest are competing successfully, not only with long established gas-works, but with petroleum. Very little of the current, however, is used for power purposes, and conveniences like the fan motors now running daily by the hundred thousand in the United States are well-nigh unknown; so much so that when needed they are shipped from New York. In Berlin 19.9 per cent. of the current is employed in lighting dwellings and hotels, but in Hamburg the same item runs up to 38.7 per cent. Store lighting in the larger German and Austrian cities averages 80 per cent. of the current. Berlin and Vienna use much less than 10 per cent. of the current for driving motors in factories, stores, etc. Exceedingly little use is yet made of the current for heating. A large proportion of the stations have storage-battery equipments; in America this auxiliary is almost unheard of in central-station operation, though nobody appears to know why.

New York, May 27. — Some of the most important devices used for the transmission of electricity for lighting purposes are involved in an application for an injunction to be argued in the United States Circuit Court to-day. The Westinghouse Electric Manufacturing Company is seeking to enjoin The Stanley Electric Manufacturing Company, asserting that patents of Nikola Tesla have been infringed. The counsel who will appear in the argument includes former Speaker Thomas B. Reed, Charles E. Mitchell, formerly United States Commissioner of Patents, and William Houston Kenyon.
The present suit is the seventh one brought to test the validity of these patents, and upon the outcome vast Interests are dependent. The legal papers to be used in the case fill several bulky volumes, going over in great detail the history of the inventions in dispute.

Dr. Humphries So Characterizes Proposed Tesla Plan.
Dr. H. R. Humphries, neurologist at the Post Graduate Hospital, does not think very highly of Nikola Tesla's scheme to improve the mental condition of defective children by electric stimulation. As a neurologis for ten years at the Vanderbilt Clinic and for five years at the State Hospital for the Insane, Dr. Humphries has had experience with mental diseases and he feels very strongly on this particular subject.
"As I understand the proposed scheme," he said, "the plan is to charge the walls of the schoolroom where the defective children are with electricity and so to set up in the air a high grade frequency current. It is believed that this current will stimulate the cerebral cells of the defective child and so improve mentality. The proposition is silly.
"In my opinion, based upon years of ob- servations and experiment, there would be no value in such a proceeding. If we thought there was any value in it we could supply every defective child at our hospitals with a skull cap in which could be set up such a high grade frequency current, but we know that there would be no use in trying it. That would be to overestimate the therapeutic value of electricity.

Oswego Daily Palladium
April 9th, 1896
Page number(s):
8
Governor Morton Invited to Attend an Exhibition.
ALBANY, April 9. — Frank W. Hawley was here to-day and extended to Gov. Morton an invitation to be present and officiate at the opening of the National Exposition of Electrical Appliances, to be held at the Grand Central Palace, in the city of New York on May 5th.
The Governor’s part in the great event will be the turning on of a current of electricity generated at the Falls of Niagara and transmitted a distance of 472 miles over one of the commercial wires of the Western Union telegraph, the new “Tesla” system of long distance transmission being employed.
The current will operate a large model of the Niagara power plant and a model of the cable-way system of canal boat propulsion. This is the longest transmission of power ever accomplished. The nearest approach to it was a transmission over a line in Europe 110 miles long.
Another feature of the exposition as explained to the Governor will be the placing of a large receiver at the brink of the Falls and a transmitter in the exposition building, enabling those witnessing the application of this mysterious energy to the movement of machinery to hear the roar of the great cataract that produces it.

"For more than eighteen years I have experimented with the atmospheric effects of electrical discharges of tremendous strength. While I am not familiar with the experiments along this line of anyone else, I have no hesitancy in declaring that the next step in the mastery of man over Nature will be the absolute control of the weather."
This statement, made by Nikola Tesla admittedly one of the greatest electricians of the age, when told of the recent experiments looking toward the control of the weather by electricity made by John A. Grahme.
"Atmospheric effects, such as Mr. Grahme claims to be able to produce," continued Mr. Tesla, "necessitate the production of electrical discharges far beyond any that have yet been obtained by artificial means. An Electrical Convention
New York Times
August 21st, 1889
Page number(s):
2
At the last meeting of the Connell of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers the action of the preceding meeting was reviewed, and instead of a committee of five, the President was directed to appoint a committee of fifteen to form a plan of organization for an international electrical convention to be held in this city coincident with the World's Fair of 1892. Secretary R. W. Pope was instructed to inform President Mascart of the electrical conference at Paris of this action, and to suggest that the unfinished work of the present conference be taken up at the proposed conference of 1892.
The following were elected delegates to represent the institute at the Paris conference now in session: Thomas A. Edison, E. Wilbur Rice, Jr., Carl Hering, Joseph Wetzler, and Nikola Tesla. All of them are now in France or on the way there. President Elihu Thompson will in a few days announce his appointments on the committee of fifteen and the work of organization will then be taken up. An invitation will be extended to all the electrical organizations of the country to participate in the proposed international conference.

Electrical Exhibition in New York
Cortland Standard
May 15th, 1896

2
The present electrical exhibition in New York is the most important and interesting of the kind ever held. Among its main features will be exhibited for the first time on a large scale Tesla's invention for telegraphing around the world without a wire or metallic circuit. If it is successful, the world will need no more telegraph poles or ocean cables. Tesla has also succeeded in producing an electrical current of 10,000,000 volts, which he declares is perfectly harmless. The sight of machinery whirling and spinning by means of power brought from Niagara falls, 450 miles away, is enough to make anybody be thankful he lives in this age and generation. Edison's fluoroscope, in which the visitor may see the skeleton frame of his hands and arms, is calculated tο make one feel creepy.

They Expect Edison, Tesla and Pupin at Their Convention
Great Barrington, Mass, June 18. — The first detachment of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, who are to hold their annual convention here the present week, arrived by special train from New York. There were 100 engineers in the party. An additional hundred will arrive when the convention will be called to order in the town hall.
The entire early summer colony turned out to meet the engineers at the railway station. There was an interminable procession of carriages and the local committer, comprising the principal citizens of the town, was kept busy assorting the engineers and sending them away to their respective hotels.
The convention will hold morning sessions daily until Saturday, when the engineers will return to New York, on a special train. It is expected that Thomas A. Edison, Nicola Tesla and Professor Pupin will be present. The Town Hall is beautifully decorated with evergreens and electric bulbs in honor of the occasion.
Many important papers are to be read to the convention and many new theories are to be aired. Among the authors to be heard are several young aspirants to the mantles of Edison, Pupin and Tesla.

A Electrical Genius
New York Press
April 3rd, 1892
Page number(s):
22
Nikola Tesla was born at Smiljan, a small place on the Austrian border, and is now 35 years of age. His education was received at Carlstadt in Croatia; he showed the experimental beat, and eventually entered the polytechnic school in Gratz, Austria. Here he studied engineering and devoted his spare time to studying electricity. On graduation he entered the engineering department of the telegraph at Budapest. His recent lectures before European authorities and his ingenious electrical inventions have made him famous. His New York laboratory is one of the best equipped in the country.

Half-tone Picture Transmitted by Wire from Chicago to New York.
NEW YORK, April 13. — Two bodies of scientific men gathered last night — one in Columbia College, this city, and the other in the rooms of the Quadrangle in Chicago, to witness the test of an electrical Instrument which was to transmit the half-tone picture by wire of President Seth Low to the Chicagoans and that of President Harris to the New Yorkers. The experiment was a success at the New York end, and 8,000 people gathered in the hall and watched the features of the President of the Chicago University evolve out of a maze of pin points in tin foil till it became a facsimile of the one on the transmitter, 1,000 miles away.
Chicagoans Disappointed
The Chicago audience however, according to word received by telegraph, was disappointed. The instrument at that end did not work because of heavy Induction in the wires.
R. H. Palmer operated the electrical machine transmitting the picture. The instrument contains tin foil perforated with countless pin holes each containing a separate wire. The paper upon which the picture is produced is wrapped around a cylinder upon which the sensitive tin foil stylus makes the ink dots corresponding in light and shade to the half-tone picture being transmitted.

The wonders of electricity have often been discussed with lively interest. This has been called the electrical age, because of the extraordinary developments in applying the subtle current to practical and beneficent purposes. But evidently we are only in the initial stages of electrical progress. No one has attained greater prominence in this line of activity than Nikola Tesla. Hence what he says, even if clothed in what seems to the average reader the language of extravagance, is certain to command attention.

Electrical Phenomena
Progressive Batavian
1893
In one of his remarkable lectures, Tesla states that most scientific men now look upon the various forms of manifestations of energy, which are generally designated "electric," as energy manifestations of the same nature as those of radiant heat and light. The phenomena of light and heat, and others besides, may therefore be called electrical phenomena, and thus it is that electrical science has become the mother science of all, and its study all-important. The day when we shall know exactly what electricity is will chronicle an event probably greater and of more moment than any other recorded in the history of the human race.

Electrical Possibilities
Geneva Advertiser
May 14th, 1894
Electrical Possibilities. It is not an extravagant statement to say that never before in the history of the world has there been a scientific discovery about which centered such magnificent dreams as are being built up on certain recently discovered electrical principles. "Among these the foremost place," says the Springfield Republican , must be given to the astounding discoveries of the young Serbian genius, Nikola Tesla, which are so novel and so extraordinary that the most imaginative of inventors are unable to foresee what form their development will take. Just as experimenters were beginning to think that they knew all that could be learned about electricity, and that further improvement must be in the line of more perfect mechanical application, Mr. Tesla shows us the electric fluid under conditions in which it differs from ordinary electricity as much as light differs from heat. A current of 2,000 volts will kill a man in the twinkling of an eye, but this modern wizard lets currents pour through his hands with a potential of 200,000 volts, vibrating 1,000,000 times a second and showering from him in dazzling streams of light. For some time after the experiment ceases his body and clothing emit streams and halos of splintered light.

A Cable for Each 5,000 Horse-power Will be Laid — Many Points Are Yet to be Determined Upon as to the Apparatus to be Used.
Prof. George Forbes, the celebrated English electrical expert, is a recent arrival in this country. He is the consulting electrical engineer for the great Niagara Falls tunnel, and to a reporter for the Electrical Review he has been telling some interesting facts about the development and transmission of the power. “What kind of generators will you use?”
“Well, for Buffalo distribution we shall undoubtedly use the alternating current system, but as regards the local plants, we have not made up our minds whether the current shall be continuous or alternating. Tesla says that coal will not play so important a part in producing the power of the earth as wood does now, and shows an invention of his in the experimental stage, about which he declares that there is no possibility of its failure. He declares that the apparatus is so simple that the least learned in mechanics can comprehend it, and if it were fully described others might seize his idea, patent it, and control a blessing which he intends shall be a free gift to the world. This is so extraordinary, so totally at variance with established customs, that it is almost as unbelievable as the discovery itself.
In the center of a large room with a glass roof Tesla will place a huge cylinder of thick glass on a bed of asbestos, supported by a firm stone pedestal placed in the center of the room. The circle will be laid lengthwise, and will be surrounded by a circle of mirrors covered with asbestos coats to refract the rays of the sun into the glass cylinder. The cylinder will always be kept full of water, which will have been treated by a secret chemical process, which Tesla claims to have devised, and which, he says, is the only complicated part of the discovery. Mining and Scientific Press
February 2nd, 1895

Tesla's latest invention, the "Oscillator," is described as one of the most remarkable appliances of the age, consisting of "the core of a steam engine and the core of a dynamo combined, making a harmonious mechanical adjustment." This combination, says an enthusiastic admirer, constitutes a machine which has in it the potentiality of reducing to the rank of old bell metal half the machinery at present moving on the face of the globe. It may come to do the entire work of the engines of an ocean steamship within the small space they occupy and at a fraction of their cost, both of construction and operation. It will do this work without jar or pounding, and will reduce to a minimum the risk of derangement or breakage. There is nothing in the whole range of mechanical construction, from railway locomotives to stamp mills, which such an invention may not revolutionize. The essential characteristic of the machine is the application of the pressure of steam to produce the extremely rapid vibration of a bar of steel, or piston, which, in turn, is so adapted to a set of magnets that the mechanical energy of the vibration is converted into electricity. Copper Producing interests present Engraved Cube of Metal Weighing 486 Pounds.
EXHIBITION IS STARTED WITH FORMAL LUNCHEON
Gift to "Wizard" Records Great Increase in Copper Output Due to Uses of Electricity.
Presenting a cubic foot of copper to Mr. Thomas A. Edison to-day at the luncheon which opened the Electrical Exposition at the New Grand Central Palace, the copper producing interests recognized the inventor’s service to them in expanding the copper industry by the extensive use of copper since the beginning of the electrical age. Mr. Edison sat at the principal place at the speakers’ table to-day, while an American flag was removed from a pedestal before him, exposing the perfect cube of copper, weighing 486 pounds. It is the first block of that size ever cast and required six castings to produce the perfect specimen, beautifully finished and engraved, and mounted on an ebony pedestal.
Some time ago, when conversing with some representatives of the copper industry, Mr. Edison jokingly remarked that they ought to present him with some token to show their appreciation of his inventions having boomed the sale of copper. Gloversville Daily Leader
March 3rd, 1896
Tesla is as deep in the subtleties of electricity as any man, but he says the new photographic light is a complete surprise to him, and a matter of great scientific importance.
In France, hospitals for infectious diseases are furnished with telephones, so that the sick may converse with their friends without danger of communicating disease.
It appears that after a thorough investigation the old underground railway company of London, England, has decided to replace its steam engines with electric locomotives.
Dr. G. M. Jenison, of Minneapolis, Minn., reports that electricity has been successfully employed by him in checking hemorrhage from the extraction of teeth. The current, he states, caused instant coagulation of the blood, and gave relief where the usual remedies were without effect.
According to a French journal of a recent date, an electric arrangement has been devised which consists of a microphone placed near the head of a baby in its cradle, and connected to a sort of relay which operates an electric bell placed near to where the nurse is asleep — a cry from the child will therefore cause the bell to ring.

An Electrical Wizard
Utica Sunday Tribune
March 19th, 1893
Nikola Tesla Allows a Charge of 200,000 Volts to Pass Through His Body.
"I am convinced that I can today send a message to a ship at sea, and that those on board can understand it. If I cannot, I am willing to lay my head on the guillotine."
Nikola Tesla.
It was Nikola Tesla who made the above strange remark, and his wonderful achievements in the development of electrical science make his words worthy of respectful consideration. He has already established the fact that but one wire is necessary to create an electrical current and is now engaged on the problem of transmitting a current without the use of a wire at all. That he has grasped the secret of how this may ultimately be accomplished some of the experiments exhibited at his public lectures would seem to demonstrate.
Tesla produces a distinct and powerful glow without the aid of wires or globes and with apparatus remarkable chiefly for its simplicity. This consists of two highly charged disks; between which the light appears without a connecting fila ment of any kind. In an incandescent lamp hung on a single wire, but not connected with it, he produces a red light almost blinding in its brilliancy, which becomes a powerful white on increasing the frequency of alternations in the current. Electrical World
February 15th, 1890
Page number(s):
106
While a large portion of the European family has been surging westward during the last three or four hundred years, settling the vast continents of America, another, but smaller, portion has been doing frontier work in the Old World, protecting the rear by beating back the "unspeakable Turk" and reclaiming gradually the fair lands that endure the curse of Mohammedan rule. For a long-time the Slav people - who, after the battle of Kosovopolje, in which the Turks defeated the Servians, retired to the confines of the present Montenegro, Dalmatia, Herzegovina and Bosnia and "Borderland" of Austria - knew what it was to deal, as our Western pioneers did, with foes ceaselessly fretting against their frontier; and the races of these countries through their strenuous struggle against the armies of the Crescent, have developed notable qualities of bravery and sagacity, while maintaining a patriotism and independence unsurpassed in any other nation.
It was in this interesting border region and from among these valiant Eastern folk that Nikola Tesla was born; and the fact that he, to-day, finds himself in America and is one of our foremost electricians is striking evidence of the extraordinary attractiveness alike of electrical pursuits and of the country where electricity enjoys its widest application.

In the Electrical World - Tesla's Remarkable Lecture
Progressive Batavian
1893
In one of his remarkable lectures, Tesla states that most scientific men now look upon the various forms of manifestations of energy, which are generally designated “electric,” as energy manifestations of the same nature as those of radiant heat and light. The phenomena of light and heat, and others besides, may therefore be called electrical phenomena, and then it is that electrical science has become the mother science of all, and its study all-important. The day when we shall know exactly what electricity is will chronicle an event probably greater and of more moment than any other recorded in the history of the human race.

Electricians in This City Regard the Hunter Patents as Amusing
New York Herald
December 22nd, 1897
Page number(s):
3
Electricians in this city do not take Rudolph M. Hunter seriously. They say he will patent anything regardless of its practicability, and probably ranks seventh among men and corporations in the number of his patented electrical devices. He is credited with having taken out more than four hundred patents.
I explained to Nikola Tesla, in his laboratory at No. 46 East Houston street, yesterday. Mr. Hunter's latest patents. He was greatly amused.
"I could tell a whole lot about Mr. Hunter and his numerous patents," he said, "but it might appear that I am antagonistic to him, which is not so.
"His contention that his patents cover the alternating principle of transmitting electrical energy is silly. This method dates too far back to be patented as a system. I do not think his claims will prove an important factor in the electrical world or a disturbing element in the methods now in use."
At the offices of the Westinghouse Company, No. 120 Broadway. Mr. Hunter's patents were treated as amusing.
"We know Mr. Hunter very well," said Mr. Terry, the patent attorney of the company. "These transformer patents amount to little. We own six thousand of the ten thousand patents covering electrical devices. We are working under them and shall continue to work under them."

Tesla Gives Demonstrations of His Latest Invention.
TRANSMITTING PICTURES BY WIRE
Test Fails Because of Induction, but Success Hoped for Today — Edison and John D. Rockefeller Present.
Of more than usual interest to the general public is the conversazione held yesterday in Columbia University by the American Institute of Electrical Engineers. Many new and important inventions were shown and original and interesting experiments were made. The exhibits fill twelve rooms and represent the work of fifty eminent scientists. Among them is Nikola Tesla.
Interest last night centred in an effort to transmit pictures to distant cities by wire. The receiving point was the University of Chicago. The test failed, so it was reported from Chicago.
The instrument, or electrograph, had worked successfully across distances of several hundred miles, but last night, owing to induction of the wires in New York, would not record the thousand of fine dots of which the pictures are composed. It was proposed to transmit between the two cities pictures of President William R. Harper of the University of Chicago, President Seth Low of Columbia and John D. Rockefeller.

It is a modification of the old tape printing “ticker,” which the general public has so long seen in use in hotels, banks and brokers’ offices to record stock transactions and such other news as is generally bulletined in that way. The “page printer” uses pretty much the same little wheel to do the printing. In place of the tape of narrow paper a continuous roll a little wider than two columns of the Sun is automatically fed in front of this wheel and prints in a broad line of clear type whatever the matter is that is to be published. This roll of news can be 2 inches, 2 feet or two yards long, or any other length desired. An expert telegrapher is now needed to send out the messages, which are printed simultaneously on all the instruments on the circuit. Electricity and Disease
Oswego Daily Palladium
January 28th, 1896
Page number(s):
4
There may be something in the report that Nikola Tesla has discovered a way in which diseases may be shaken out of the human system by electricity. Last week a New York electrician accidentally made himself a conductor for a current of electricity with an estimated strength of 2,000 volts, or 300 more volts than is developed by the machines at Sing Sing which electrocute condemned murderers. As will be seen by the account printed of the accident printed on our seventh page to-day, the electrician was thrown into convulsions by the shock, and for an entire day his life hung in the balance. But when he recovered he pronounced himself as feeling better than he did before the accident. He is experiencing a feeling of rejuvenation, like that which follows a long rest, and has lost a stubborn case of rheumatism which was the cause of much pain and suffering.
While the victim of the electrical accident was slowly recovering his equilibrium, the section on general medicine of the New York Academy of Medicine was discussing “The Theory and Treatment of Rheumatism,” and expressing opinions as to the cause of the disease. This discussion revealed the fact that the medical profession is inclining to the belief that rheumatism is caused by bacteria in the blood. Electricity and Wires
Yonkers Statesman
August 31st, 1900
Page number(s):
1
A patent has been granted to Nikola Tesla for an invention which, if his claims are borne out, will prevent the escape of electricity from a wire. Tesla's invention, it is claimed, solves the insulation problem in a simple manner. He insulates the wire by passing through it, or near it, air kept at a low temperature, producing a coat of ice on the wire, which, the inventor finds, cannot be broken through by the strongest current, and at the same time gives an insulation that costs practically nothing. By means of this latest discovery the loss of electricity or electrical energy in transmission, it is claimed, can be rendered so small as to be insignificant, and power can be transmitted to great distances by means of underground wires.

Electricity on the Canal
Clyde Democratic Herald
November 8th, 1893
The test of electricity as a motor power on the canals of the State will probably be made at Pittsford on the Erie Canal near Rochester, Saturday, November 11th. The pole line is already completed and the generators and electrical appliances have been shipped from Pittsburg to Pittsford. The experiment will be witnessed by State officials, officers of the Niagara Power Company and officers of the Westinghouse Electrical Company, who will arrive at Pittsford at 9 a. m. on the day of the experiment, on a West Shore special train leaving New York at 10 o’clock the night before.
Mr. F. W. Hawley, who is actively interested in the experiment and whose residence is at Pittsford, received a dispatch this morning to the effect that the experimental boat, the first electrical canal boat ever built, is at Buffalo. It will probably reach Pittsford Monday. Nikola Tesla, the great Hungarian electrician from Budapest, and George Forbes, the celebrated English electrician, will be present to study this new application of electricity.

Electricity from Coal
New York Globe
November 26th, 1904
Page number(s):
3
The Dynelectron and Other Carbon Batteries — A Long Series of Failures — Attempts by Tesla and Edison — The Probability of Eventual Success.
The revolutionary character and vast financial possibilities of a practical commercial battery producing electricity directly from coal, without the intervention of boiler and steam engine, is obvious enough to the merest tyro in mechanics. Theoretically, such a coal battery might have an efficiency of something like 70 per cent., whereas existing methods of producing electrical energy, according to W. R. Cooper, only render available 6 per cent. of the energy of the coal. This fact, combined with the possibility of greatly reducing the cost of an electric plant, through the elimination of engines, boilers, and a number of the skilled workmen necessary to keep them in running order, makes the coal battery an intensely fascinating problem for the inventor.
However, despite the numerous attempts made to solve it, only dismal failure has hitherto been the result. The latest of these is called by its inventor, J. H. Reid of Newark, N. J., the dynelectron. This machine and Mr. Reid himself are described at considerable length in the October number of the Marconigram. From the facts stated there the dynelectron seems to be, in its essentials, an iron box divided into three compartments. In two of these caustic soda is placed.

BY FRANZ BENDT.
TRANSLATED FOR "THE CHAUTAUQUAN" FROM THE GERMAN "UEBER LAND UND MEER."
It is mostly through its practical results that a science appeals to the general public for anything more than a casual attention. This fact is nowhere more noticeable than in electricity, which has loaded humanity with gifts and in a comparatively short time has revolutionized customs and business so that the present era not unjustly has been called "the age of electricity." The term is doubly appropriate because, as all signs indicate, we are not at the end but only just at the beginning of the electrical epoch. Moreover, it should be noted, the wonderful and mysterious manner in which the electrical forces are manifested have thoroughly aroused astonishment, even in adepts, and a thirst for knowledge in the laity.

July 15th, 1893

The following will be the weekly schedule of lectures upon the Electricity Department of the World’s Fair. They will be delivered at 10 o’clock each day in the Agricultural Assembly Hall by Prof. Gooch.
On Mondays there will be discussed the principles of primary batteries, storage batteries, electric furnace, electro-plating, electric engraving, and Edison’s last invention, the Kinetograph.
Tuesdays — The telegraph, telephone, phonograph, telautograph, Atlantic cable system, and cooking and heating.
Wednesdays — Edison system of lighting.
Thursdays — The alternating system and Nikola Tesla’s theory of utilizing the power of Niagara Falls.
Fridays — Arc lighting, welding and drilling.
Saturdays — Electric street car system.
The purpose of the lectures is to give an intelligent understanding of the principles of the various apparatus on exhibition, the manner of their construction and practical operation. The class is open to all persons who desire an explanation of the wonderful developments of electricity and the various applications to which it may be adapted.

An interesting example of electric-power transmission is that of the Gold King stamp-mill near Telluride, Col. A Pelton wheel, receiving water through a two-foot steel pipe under 320 feet head, drives the generator at a speed of 833 revolutions, giving 10,000 alternations per minute. The generator, by an automatic compensation, is made to maintain a constant pressure of 3000 volts at the motor, three miles distant. The line runs 2500 feet directly up the mountain from the power station, and thence passes over a rough, and in winter almost inaccessible, country, to the mill. The working motor, being of the synchronous type, requires a special device for starting it, and this is furnished by a small auxiliary motor of the Tesla type. The operation of starting is accomplished by one man in about two minutes. The economical efficiency of the synchronous motor system, exclusive of loss in conductors, is found to be 83.5 per cent. at full load and 74 per cent. at half load. The capacity of the motor is 50 horse-power. Electricity Without Heat
New York Telegram
February 25th, 1897
Nikola Tesla Says the Carbon Demonstrations of Mr. Case Are Not New.
Willard E. Case's announcement before the New York Electrical Society at Columbia College that he can produce electricity from carbon without heat has caused some stir among the men who are devoting their time to the development of electricity.
He cited the fact that the generation of energy through heat involves a waste of more than 75 per cent, and that all electricity except that produced by water power or galvanic battery is obtained ultimately from carbon.
Nikola Tesla was seen to-day and asked what his views were concerning Mr. Case's new road to electricity.
"The process of converting the energy of combining carbon and oxygen with electricity without any loss in the battery is not new," he said, "It has been observed that In the process there is no weakening of temperature shown, consequently there seems to be no loss in heat.
"In my opinion this does not show at all there is no loss in reaching a combination. On the contrary, I am convinced that the second law of thermo-dynamics is far more general than it is believed to be. As long, however, as we contine ourselves to developing energy by consuming material we are adhering to barbarous processes which imply destruction and waste.

Electricity Without Wires
by Nikola Tesla
New York Herald
January 1st, 1896
TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD: —
In reply to your question as to what discovery would do most to better our condition, in my opinion the demonstration that the earth's electrical charge can be distributed, and thereby electrical waves efficiently transmitted to any distance without the use of cables or wires, would be the most beneficial.
The conveying of motive power from sources such as Niagara in this manner to any place, however remote, would increase many times the productive capacity of mankind. It would bring millions of miserable creatures from the darkness of the coal pits to the light of day. It would cause a kinder feeling to spring up between the weak and the strong, which would lead to a generous adjustment of the evermore difficult questions of labor and capital.
Even if power could not be distributed, the mere transmission of intelligible signals would be of incalculable benefit. Such a realization would do away. with the instability of the financial markets, which is the cause of much suffering and misery. It would greatly facilitate the evolution of novel ideas, as well as the prevention of evils. It would increase the safety of travel and give a new impetus to the press and spread of knowledge. Western Electrician
October 7th, 1893
Page number(s):
179-180
Awards formed the principal topic of discussion among the electrical exhibitors at the World's Fair last week. The exclusive publication of the list in the Western Electrician excited much interest, and the paper was in great demand. The comments were many and varied. Some exhibitors were jubilant; others were angry and disgusted, while not a few professed indifference, with the remark, "What do the awards amount to, anyway?" It was noticeable, however, that all seemed eager to secure the diplomas and medals before the list was posted. Many, also, were puzzled by the fact that several awards, in a number of cases, were given on one class of apparatus. This is explained by the fact that the judges did not consider the comparative merits of. exhibits in making awards. They examined each exhibit entered for an award separately, and if, in, their judgment, the article or group was found to be worthy of commendation an award was given it, the specific points of excellence being detailed in the diploma. It thus happened that on the commoner sorts of apparatus, such as arc lamps, for instance, a number of awards were given on the same class of exhibits, although the exact language of the awards, specifying the points of excellence, will not be alike on any two diplomas. Aside from several distinguished members of the congress who remained to see the exposition, two notable figures attracted attention in the electricity building last week — Thomas A. Edison and Nikola Tesla. Mr. Edison paid several visits to the building, strictly in the capacity of a spectator, and greatly enjoyed his inspection of the exhibits. Mr. Tesla gave a number of experiments before invited guests and the general public. On Tuesday afternoon he repeated, at the agricultural assembly hall, the substance of his lecture on "Mechanical and Electrical Oscillators," which was delivered before the members of the congress on the preceding Friday. On this occasion he had for an audience von Helmholtz and a number of other scientists who had been unable to attend the first lecture. On Tuesday evening Mr. Tesla repeated his beautiful and interesting high tension and high frequency experiments in the dark pavilion of the Westinghouse company in electricity building before a number of foreign engineers, including W. H. Preece, H. D. Wilkinson, MM. Mascart and de la Touanne, Dr. Lobach, F. W. Tischendoerfer and others. Electricity's New Marvels
New York Press
April 18th, 1896
Many Will Be Seen at the National Exhibition Next Month.
Many interesting features have been arranged for the opening of the National Electric Exhibition on May 4 at the Grand Central Palace. Governor Morton has been asked to officiate. Electric power will be sent by the Tesla system over a Western Unton wire from Niagara Falls, a distance of 462 miles. The power will be used for the operation of a model of the Niagara power system, as well as for sending a message of congratulation from the President to Queen Victoria on her birthday.
The lines of the Portal Telegraph and Cabie Company will be offered for the transmission of the Niagara power across the continent.

Portville Review
October 17th, 1912
The secret of the universe is the secret of electricity.
"The New Knowledge" is the term used for designating the revelations which came with the study of radium and radio-activity. "The New Knowledge" has taught us that matter — lead, stone, wood, hydrogen, oxygen, everything and anything which we call matter — is nothing but electricity.
An atom of hydrogen consists of a thousand "electrons" — mere charges of electricity. An atom of lead consists of some hundreds of thousands of such "electrons'. That is why hydrogen is so light and lead so heavy. Each is drawn to that great mass of matter, the earth, in proportion to the number of electric charges which make up the earth. That is the law of gravitation. It is all a question of electricity.
We ourselves are nothing but collections of "electron" of many sorts. The rose in the bosom of beauty, and the bone in the jaws of the Beast, are like the Beauty and the Beast, nothing but greater or lesser, simpler or more complex collection of "electrons" or electric charges. Matter studied closely vanishes in matterless electricity.
